stem: What happens to RAM (Random Access Memory) when you turn off your computer?

options.text: It saves everything automatically to the hard drive
Everything stored in RAM is lost
RAM keeps the data for 24 hours
RAM transfers to the CPU for safekeeping

explanation_after: RAM is volatile memory — it only works while electricity flows through it. The moment power cuts, every byte in RAM vanishes. This is why you must save files to disk (non-volatile storage) before closing your laptop. This distinction matters enormously in AI: model weights must be loaded from disk into RAM every time you run inference.

stem: A large language model has 7 billion parameters, each stored as a 16-bit float (2 bytes). Approximately how much RAM does it need just to hold the weights?

options.text: About 70 MB
About 700 MB
About 14 GB
About 1.4 TB

explanation_after: 7 billion × 2 bytes = 14 GB. This is why running a 7B model requires a GPU with at least 14 GB of VRAM. Understanding memory math is essential for practical AI engineering — it tells you whether a model will even fit on your hardware.

stem: Which analogy best compares RAM with permanent storage?

options.text: RAM is a filing cabinet; storage is a desk
RAM is a desk; storage is a filing cabinet
RAM is a keyboard; storage is a monitor
RAM and storage are both temporary desks

explanation_after: The desk/filing cabinet analogy is the standard mental model for RAM vs storage. You work on things at your desk (RAM), and when done, file them away (storage). AI models are loaded from storage (filing cabinet) into RAM (desk) when running.

stem: Which statement correctly compares the speed and capacity of RAM versus a hard drive or SSD?

options.text: RAM is much faster to read and write than storage, but storage typically holds far more data
Storage is always faster than RAM
RAM and storage have identical speed and identical cost
RAM has effectively infinite capacity

explanation_after: RAM trades capacity for speed: it's extremely fast to access but limited in size (and volatile). Storage trades speed for capacity: it holds far more data permanently, but reading and writing to it is much slower than RAM. This tradeoff is why computers use both, rather than just one or the other.

stem: Which of the following is an example of non-volatile storage — meaning it keeps its data even without power?

options.text: RAM
CPU cache
SSD (solid-state drive)
CPU registers

explanation_after: SSDs (and hard drives) are non-volatile — data survives a power loss. RAM, CPU cache, and CPU registers are all volatile: they lose their contents the instant power is cut. This is why anything you want to keep must eventually be written to storage, not just left in RAM.

stem: Why do machine learning engineers periodically save 'checkpoints' of a model to disk during a long training run?

options.text: To make the GPU run faster
Because the model's weights live in RAM during training, and RAM is volatile — a crash or power loss would lose hours of training progress if it isn't saved to persistent storage
Checkpoints are required by Python's syntax
To reduce the size of the training dataset

explanation_after: Training a large model can take hours or days, and the weights being updated live in RAM (or GPU memory) the entire time. Because that memory is volatile, engineers periodically write ('checkpoint') the current weights to disk so a crash doesn't erase all progress — the same RAM-vs-storage tradeoff you'd apply to an unsaved document, just at a much larger scale.
